children.text: Your comment got flagged and killed; I don't know whether automated systems attempt to detect AI-generated comments. I vouched for you because the content was explicitly solicited.

Uncle Bob Martin and Matt Pocock discuss the risks of relying on AI agents without human oversight, emphasizing that unchecked code can lead to significant technical issues:

   - Accumulated Technical Debt: Uncle Bob notes that agents often leave behind "dog doo" (messy code) (05:13-05:18). If you don't clean it, the code becomes progressively worse as you build on it (11:06-11:10).
   - Loss of Agent Coherence: When code quality degrades, agents struggle to maintain direction (11:13-11:16). They may enter a loop of inadvertently breaking existing features while attempting to fix new ones, eventually leading to them failing entirely or giving up (11:22-12:04).
   - The "Trapped" Trajectory: Matt Pocock highlights the risk of a session's "trajectory" (23:18-23:45). Without intervention, an agent's initial messy approach or misaligned focus will continue throughout the entire session, reinforcing poor patterns instead of correcting them (23:35-24:00).
   - Hidden Hallucinations: Even though agents are fast, they are still prone to hallucinations and misalignment (25:09-25:18). Relying on them blindly without deterministic tools or human spot checks risks incorporating silent, logic-breaking bugs into the architecture (09:08-09:19).
Why don't you just quote them then? Or quote whatever the LLM you used gave.

children.author: sublinear

children.text:
Exactly.

I've recently finished a browser game specifically targeting an old iPad Air 1 we had lying around the house.

I had a working version after a weekend, but it took me a month to make it run smoothly on an over 10 years old mobile device. And the most recent browser available is almost 10 years old.

Surprisingly I didn't missed too many "modern" JS features, as these were mostly functional programming oriented which doesn't play well with optimization anyways, and the ES6 was more than enough as a programming platform.

Anyway, what I'm trying to say is that "the best practice" should be making your apps fast and accessible - as much as you can without having to sacrifice something you value - instead of chasing the latest and shiniest.

Don't be a fashion driven developer. :)

The "modern web primitives" are also not even necessarily the "best practice".

Browser-specific implementation gotchas tend to take about a decade to iron out for reasons that never have anything to do with code quality. Users are fickle and so are browser vendors, but that's a different topic.

At the end of the day, there's just no escaping lots of manual testing across device and browser combinations if your goal is a polished result and not just something that "works".

AI has done nothing to make this problem go away. If anything, it's made it worse because people don't even want to look at the code now!

children.text:
Spot-on amazing linking exactly to the relevant discussion.

I’m really glad to see this not evolve into a flame war as well.
These exact questions came up (from Apple) during design review. If you're interested you can read the discussion here: https://github.com/WebKit/standards-positions/issues/85#issu...

Why was 'fetchLater' chosen over a reliable way to trigger fetch from 'unload' or a similar event, or inversely, adding a 'sendLater' option to sendBeacon? Feels like a bolted-on API for a very specific use case, when the same thing could be built from better primitives?

It's a bit sad that browsers now have two different, "standard" APIs created entirely for the purpose of user tracking, as if things weren't already bloated enough.

It's currently being added to WebKit: https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/pull/73271

Regarding corporate incentives: I was involved in the design of this API, so I know the history. It was proposed many years ago as a solution to make it easier for RUM analytics providers to measure Core Web Vitals metrics that needed to account for more than just page load (e.g. layout shifts and slow interactions can happen any time, not just during page load).

The RUM providers we worked with were reluctant to wait until page unload to send telemetry data because it resulted in too many lost beacons, so what they do instead is send beacons every few seconds with the most up-to-date payload.

The `fetchLater()` API enables them to send just one beacon, which is good for users and also reduces their server load.
I think I can guess from corporate incentives why Chrome supports fetchLater and some others don't.

children.author: embedding-shape
children.text:
Maybe this mental model of yours need to include how difficult it'd be to implement your own version of the suggested API to make it actually cross-platform.

In the case of fetchLater, judging by https://nicj.net/beaconing-in-practice-fetchlater/ (which I think you intended to link actually) since I haven't come across it before, it could be implemented with fetchLater, events and a timeout, perhaps 10 LOC or so? If that's the case, then it almost never makes sense to use Chrome's own fetchLater, rather than those ~10 LOC so it's actually web-friendly instead of just Chrome friendly.

As a side-note, I'm getting increasingly wary about all the new JS APIs that seemingly gets added to our standards ONLY because they have ads/tracking interests. Used to be the people who participated in standards discussions for their ads/tracking interests came up with proper use cases and kept quiet about their erosion of privacy, but seems the mask is fully off today and we're just making browser engines for the ads companies now, yay.

Agreed the line can be blurry, but I want to stress that the goal of this project is NOT to push Chrome-only APIs on users.

The mental model we've been using on the team is:

If you hired an expert web development consultant to build X, what would they recommend as a best practice? When does it make sense to use the new API (because it provides real benefits) vs. when does it make sense to wait until it's available everywhere?

To use your `fetchLater()` example, this is a case where the `fetchLater()` API legitimately solves a very real problem for people trying to build accurate analytics or telemetry features, see: https://nicj.net/beaconing-in-practice/

And lots of companies actually are already using `fetchLater()` in production now because of its increased reliability.

The line between documenting and instructing is blurry in many cases. For example, these statements are meant to document best practices to the agent, but they sound like instructions:

"DO use fetchLater()..."

"Your own code MUST call fetchLater() directly..."

https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/mai...

But yes, the skills do document compatibility and fallbacks well.

So if that's universally applied it might not be so unreasonable, but I don't do much frontend dev to know whether it's worth the risk or not.

> That's fine though. Progressive enhancement, adding features to a site when they're available but still offering a working site when they're not, is how we should build web sites.

Alright, that's fine and dandy. Is this the actual results of using this skill though that is being advertised here? Is it asking the agent to also make sure it's "Progressive enhancement" so the same stuff more or less works in Firefox and Safari?

If not, your whole point is kind of moot, as you have someone from Google trying to get people to write websites that'll look and/or work differently in Chrome compared to other browsers.

Here's a list of browser features the skills will tell your agent to use that are stable in Chrome but not supported by Firefox and Safari

That's fine though. Progressive enhancement, adding features to a site when they're available but still offering a working site when they're not, is how we should build web sites. That way they work for the user's device rather than the developer's opinion of what the web should do.

Working that way completely removes the decision about whether or not to use a feature because it doesn't work for some people, and moves it to a decision about whether or not it's worth adding for the users on browsers that can use it. In the past that was a real development effort cost, but today where AI writes the code the effort is much, much lower.

If you're using AI to make something but still using heuristics designed to save coding time then you really need to rethink your mental model of how to decide what gets built.

Websites created today should all use server-loaded content for the first render, small page sizes, a sub-1s loading time, progress enhancement for features, and WCAG 3.1 AAA accessibility (maybe.. at least AA though) because doing that isn't any more effort than not doing it.

In my book, new "baseline" CSS features that handle common design tasks count as simpler (and more user-friendly) than involving JavaScript to set them up, even if it's "vanilla" JS. The user's browser should as much as possible be treating my content as data rather than code and just doing fancy rendering on it, as long as I'm not explicitly trying to show the user a cool program. The browser may be huge, but it's only one thing that has to be huge for the benefit of every site.

(I have much the same instinct about the UNIX philosophy. Bash is not too big. Shell programs should be even bigger so that query programs can be smaller — because otherwise they grow huge lists of options that largely overlap, for things like table formatting, and provide an inconsistent UX.)

Remeber, the features you don't use are the ones you don't have to support, or scramble to replace when they are deprecated.

Keep your effing websites simple.

children.text:
> But most sites don't have a policy like that.

My experience differs from yours. It's true that there is some tiny fraction of features where it makes sense to do progressive enhancement, but for most sites and almost all features this does not make sense: the burden of testing and maintaining a site that effectively has multiple versions depending on what browser you're using is simply not worth it. For typical dev teams outside of Google/Meta/similar, the right thing (and the overwhelmingly common thing) is to target the intersection of features available on your supported browsers and not make any behavior conditional. I'm not interested in any guides that need fallbacks on any of the browsers I target and I expect the same is true of the typical dev team outside Google.

If your feature use policy is that you will never use any feature unless it's supported in at least X, Y, and Z browsers, then yes something like this would be possible. But most sites don't have a policy like that.

Most sites are willing to use some features as a progressive enhancement, whereas other features they won't even consider using unless it's in 99+% of their users' browsers.

And unfortunately there's no easy way to make that decision for users on a feature-by-feature basis, because it all depends on what use case they're trying to accomplish, and what will happen if the feature is not available (given that particular use case).

So our approach is to (1) explain in the guide how to implement the use case with the modern feature, (2) explain why the modern feature is the preferred solution (e.g. what the user benefit is), and then (3) explain how to implement a fallback solution if the feature is not available.

I think we could potentially experiment with some version of what you're describing, like a config option where we only surface guides that have robust, widely-available fallbacks, and where we have high confidence that it makes sense for the majority of sites to be following the recommendations in the guide.

I'll raise it with the team.

> This should work today (though not exactly in the way you describe). The skill tells the agent how to interpret guides based on browser support signals it gets from context (e.g. the prompt itself, or AGENTS.md).

Right, my point is that I don't want to spend a bunch of time and tokens loading the skills and having the agent reason through whether they apply based on browser support. I want that to be automated so that it only loads in the first place those things that are actually applicable. Having a prose description is not a substitute for automation; it is almost always better to do things mechanically rather than asking the agent to do it, in cases where it is possible to do mechanically.

I think this matters even if you're at Google and tokens are free but it _definitely_ matters for the rest of us.

I prefer to have my templates in a compiled language: not passing a map of strings to a string with interpolation points, but actually "just code" by which I define HTML builders by combining templates/layouts/components in that same "just code".

Like HtmlFlow (Java/Kotlin) or kotlinx.html.

I pick Tailwind and Alpine.js to go with this approach because: I want to be SSR-first (with small JS-based improvements where they matter most) so NOT and SPA, i want the styling to be close to the HTML code that's being styled (no need to match between CSS definition and usage), and I also prefer to keep my tiny bits of JS close to the HTML it deals with (Alpine makes that easy and provides a clear path for implementing 99% of my JS needs).

Like everyone, LLMs code it for me :) But the result is easy to reason about for myself and my LLM. Little vanilla JS. No jQuery. Mostly just some HTML-bound Alpine instructions. And Tailwind everywhere. This way I can look at one place to see how it works: or CTRL-click my way to it.

body.text:
Browsers natively handle a lot of what used to take 50 lines of JS (or a dependency): `CSS.highlights` for text range highlighting without <span>s everywhere, `<dialog>` and showModal() give you backdrops and ideal focus management, `field-sizing` to auto-grow textareas as the user types.. (Something yesterday's ftrain post touched on [0])

Models know about some of these by name, but consistently won't default to using the platform-native solution and instead prefer the incumbent <div>+JS based pattern. We started an effort in Chrome to supplement coding agents with this key domain knowledge and we're shipping our 1.0 today, in collaboration with Firefox, MDN, and Edge.

200+ guides (~1.7MB) of curated, hand-crafted implementation best-practices from web experts, updated as the web evolves. (Open source, obv, so.. we'll welcome your bikeshedding ;) Readable versions here: [1]

I've spent the last 9 months obsessing over how to ship this as an agent skill + (Agentic RAG) CLI without blowing up your context window. (Or cedeing activation mechanics to MCP dynamic tool search). The skill description is minmaxed for activating on relevant frontend tasks. The RAG work I'm pretty proud of… originally a 500mb native stack down to a ~7MB pure-JS package, ~10ms search on your CPU.

We just introduced a deterministic 'legacy-scan' (trained on 30k github repos) to identify old 'n dusted patterns that your agent can modernize. (92% avg precision on held-out repos.)

People make a lot of claims about what coding agents are good/bad at. We wanted receipts, so we invested heavily in eval infra [2] to help us hill-climb, but also to identify when knowledge is common enough we can prune our guides. (Ofc, some of the things we thought AI didn't know turned out to be wrong :) We run codex/claude/agy against 200 tasks without the skill and then with.. In total ~1,700 playwright/AST-based assertions. Agents go from 55% pass unguided to 92% guided.

Try it out:

    DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 npx modern-web-guidance@latest install
    DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 npx modern-web-guidance@latest search "animate dialog modal"
    DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 npx modern-web-guidance@latest legacy-scan ./src
If you spot something wrong or weird, give us a holler!

Longer write-up on the 1.0: https://developer.chrome.com/blog/modern-web-guidance-v1
